_comment: Guided tour for Burst Variance Analysis. The tool is hand-built Qt around a DockArea, so steps target the shared action buttons by objectName suffix ({'name': 'run'} finds toolAction_run) and the dock pages by tab title. Read by chisurf.gui.widgets.tools.guided_tour.

steps.title: Compared against shot noise, never against zero
steps.text:
BVA asks whether a burst's FRET efficiency was constant while the molecule crossed the focus.

A static molecule still varies, because a finite number of photons splits randomly into donor and acceptor. So the question is not "does it vary" but "does it vary more than shot noise alone would make it".

The numbers are bigger than intuition suggests: at 5 photons per slice, a perfectly static molecule at E = 0.5 still scatters by 0.224. Six steps.

steps.title: The burst folder
steps.text:
BVA reads a finished burst-analysis folder — the bursts are already defined and this adds a per-burst column to them. Dropping the folder on this window does the same thing.

A dropped file is refused rather than silently ignored: this analysis has nothing to do with a single measurement.

await.hint: Press the folder button and choose the burst-analysis folder.

steps.title: The one number that changes everything
steps.text:
Photons per slice is the trade. Small values give many slices per burst and sensitivity to fast exchange — at the price of a noisier per-burst σ and a taller static line. Large values smooth σ and lower the line, but go blind to the fastest dynamics. 5–10 is the usual range.

The static line must be drawn for the same slice size as the data, or the comparison means nothing; ChiSurf redraws it from the value the run actually used.

Min window length is the alternative: slice by fixed time instead of fixed photon count, which is the right choice when the count rate varies strongly across a burst.

steps.title: Which detector is which
steps.text:
The donor and acceptor detectors come from the setup defined here, and this is the definition nothing downstream re-checks.

Swap them and you still get a complete, plausible BVA plot — with the population mirrored about E = ½ — and no statistic anywhere reports it. Set it against the hardware once, and confirm it on a sample whose answer you already know.

steps.title: Run it
steps.text:
Every burst is read, sliced and scored off the GUI thread; ⏹ stops it. The result is written as a bv4/ companion beside the burst tables, one row per burst, so the browser and ndX can gate on it.

Auto update re-runs whenever a setting changes. On a large folder, turn it off while you set things up.

steps.title: On the line, above it, or arching between
steps.text:
The red curve is the static line — the scatter shot noise alone produces.

On it: static on the burst timescale.
Clearly above it: excess variance — at least two FRET states visited within one burst.
An arch bridging two spots: two-state exchange. Two non-interconverting species give two separate spots on the line and no arch — that distinction is the whole point of the plot.

Then the part that decides whether the result is real. Above the line means excess variance, not conformational dynamics. Acceptor blinking or bleaching is the most common false positive — a dye going dark mid-burst is exactly the two-level signal BVA detects. Uncorrected background lifts the whole population off a line computed for pure binomial sampling. And short bursts scatter widely in both directions, so cut on photon count and read the density, not the points.

The ? button has the rest.
